source_text: Hujus memores pronuntiationis, tanquam praescriptionis, nihilominus quam stultum et impossibile sit aqua reformari tractamus. Quid utique ista materia tantae dignationis meruerit officium? Ut opinor, auctoritas liquidi elementi exigenda est. Atquin plurima suppetit, et quidem a primordio. Nam unum ex his est quae ante omnem mundi suggestum impolita adhuc specie penes Deum quiescebant: In primordio, inquit, fecit Deus coelum et terram. Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita, et tenebrae erant super abyssum, et spiritus Dei super aquas ferebatur. Habes, homo, imprimis aetatem venerari aquarum, quod antiqua substantia; dehinc dignationem, quod divini spiritus sedes, gratior scilicet caeteris tunc elementis. Nam et tenebrae totae adhuc sine cultu siderum informes, et tristis abyssus, et terra imparata, et coelum rude: solus liquor, semper materia perfecta, laeta simplex, de suo pura, dignum vectaculum Deo subjiciebat. Quid quod exinde dispositio mundi modulatricibus quodammodo aquis Deo constitit. Nam, ut firmamentum coeleste suspenderet, in medietate distinctis aquis fecit; et, ut terram aridam suspenderet, segregatis aquis expediit. Ordinato dehinc per elementa mundo cum incolae darentur, primis aquis praeceptum est animas proferre. Primus liquor quod viveret edidit ne mirum sit, in Baptismo, si aquae animare, noverunt. Nam ipsius quoque hominis figurandi opus, sociantibus aquis absolutum est. De terra materia convenit, non tamen habilis nisi humecta et succida, quam scilicet ante quartum diem segregatae aquae in stationem suam, superstite humore, limo temperarant. Si exinde universa vel plura prosequar quae de elementi istius auctoritate commemorem, quanta vis ejus aut gratia, quot ingenia, quot officia, quantum instrumentum mundo ferat; vereor ne laudes aquae potius, quam Baptismi rationes videar congregasse. Licet eo plenius docerem non esse dubitandum, si materiam, quam in omnibus rebus et operibus suis Deus disposuit, etiam in sacramentis propriis parere fecit; si quae vitam terrenam gubernat, et in coelesti procurat.
pass_a_gloss: Being mindful of this pronouncement, as if a prescription, nevertheless we treat how foolish and impossible it is for water to be reformed. What indeed has this material deserved such a great office of dignity? As I think, the authority of the liquid element must be exacted. And indeed, very many things are supplied, and indeed from the beginning. For one of these is what was among the things which, before every suggestion of the world, in an unpolished species, was at rest with God: In the beginning, He says, God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters. You have, O man, first to venerate the age of the waters, because it is an ancient substance; then the dignity, because it is the seat of the divine Spirit, more pleasing certainly than the other elements then. For also the darknesses, all still without the cultivation of the stars, unformed, and the gloomy abyss, and the unprepared earth, and the rough heaven: the liquid alone, always a perfect material, joyful, simple, pure from its own, was presenting a worthy vehicle to God. What is it that from then on the disposition of the world was established by God in some way with the moderating waters? For, in order that He might suspend the heavenly firmament, He made it with the waters distinguished in the middle; and, in order that He might suspend the dry earth, He prepared it with the waters separated. Then, with the world ordered through the elements, when inhabitants were given, a command was given to the first waters to bring forth souls. The first liquid, because it brought forth what was living, is not wonderful, in Baptism, if waters animate, they know. For also the work of forming man was completed, with the waters assisting. The material from the earth was suitable, but not however suitable unless moist and succulent, which certainly, before the fourth day, the separated waters, with the moisture surviving, had tempered into clay. If from then on I were to follow up all or most of the things which I might mention about the authority of this element, how great its power or grace, how many talents, how many offices, how much instrument it brings to the world; I fear lest I seem to have gathered the praises of water rather than the reasons of Baptism. Although I might teach more fully that it is not to be doubted, if the material, which God has arranged in all things and works of His, He has also made to serve in His own sacraments; if what governs earthly life, and procures in heavenly life.

to indicate the abundance of evidence
to convey the idea of waters having a regulating effect
to indicate the cooperative role of waters
to emphasize the magnitude of the element's authority

bible_refs.note: In the beginning, God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.

pass_b_english: Mindful of that pronouncement as if it were a binding rule, we nevertheless address how foolish and impossible it is for water to be reformed. What, after all, has this substance done to merit so great an office of dignity? In my view, we must demand the credentials of the liquid element—and they are abundant, stretching back to the very beginning. One of them is this: before the world was even sketched out, while it still lay unpolished, water was already at rest with God. "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." The earth was formless and empty, darkness covered the deep, and the Spirit of God hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:1-2). So take note, human being: first, venerate the antiquity of water, because it is an ancient substance; second, venerate its dignity, because it served as the seat of the divine Spirit—more pleasing to Him than any other element at that time. After all, the darkness was still starless and shapeless, the abyss was gloomy, the earth unready, the heavens crude. Water alone, always a perfect material—joyful, simple, pure in itself—offered itself as a worthy vehicle for God.

And from that point on, the whole ordering of the world was established by God, so to speak, through the moderating agency of water. To suspend the heavenly firmament, He separated the waters in the middle; to make the dry land appear, He gathered the waters apart. Once the world was ordered through the elements and inhabitants were assigned, the first waters received the command to bring forth living souls. Since the first liquid produced life, it is no wonder that in Baptism waters know how to animate. Even the fashioning of man was completed with water's assistance. The material came from earth, yet it was not workable unless moist and supple—clay that the separated waters, before the fourth day, had tempered with surviving moisture. If I were to go on listing all or most of the things that attest this element's authority—how great its power and grace, how many its talents and offices, how vast its service to the world—I fear I would seem to be compiling praises of water rather than reasons for Baptism. Yet I could teach more fully that there is no room for doubt: if God has arranged this material in all His works and operations, He has also made it serve in His own sacraments—since what governs earthly life also procures heavenly life.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a fluent English version that maintains the theological nuances and causal relations. The scripture citation (Genesis 1:1-2) in Pass B correctly identifies the quoted/alluded content from the Latin 'In primordio, inquit, fecit Deus coelum et terram...'.
